subject: Archaeology
title: Easter Island: The Moai Mystery
description: One-minute skill: Easter Island: The Moai Mystery.

hook.text: Nearly 900 giant stone heads stand on a remote Pacific island. The tallest is 33 feet and weighs 82 tons.

buildup.text: The Rapa Nui people carved moai from volcanic tuff and moved them miles to platforms ringing the coastline.

discovery.text: Experiments proved that moai could 'walk' — rocked back and forth with ropes by as few as 18 people.

twist.text: The popular story blames the Rapa Nui for deforesting their island.

climax.text: European slave raids and disease in the 1800s nearly wiped out the Rapa Nui.

punchline.text: We blamed the islanders for their own collapse.

quiz.question: What does new evidence suggest about Easter Island's deforestation?
options: The Rapa Nui deliberately burned forests for farmland
Rats introduced by settlers destroyed the trees, not the people
A volcanic eruption killed all vegetation on the island

details.summary: Easter Island's nearly 1,000 moai statues were carved by Polynesian settlers between 1250 and 1500 CE. The largest stands 10 meters tall and weighs 82 tons. How they were transported across the island without wheels or draft animals remains one of archaeology's most debated questions.
details.whyItMatters: Easter Island illuminates the relationship between environmental resources and cultural achievement. The story of the moai raises questions about sustainability, ambition, and the consequences of resource depletion.
takeaways: Nearly 1,000 moai were carved between 1250 and 1500 CE
The largest moai stands 10 meters tall weighing 82 tons
Transport methods without wheels remain actively debated

faq.question: How were the moai moved?
faq.answer: Experiments show that statues could be rocked and walked along roads using ropes, matching oral traditions that the moai walked. Other theories involve log rollers, sledges, or ramps. The walking method best explains the placement of fallen statues along ancient roads.

faq.question: Did Easter Islanders really destroy their environment?
faq.answer: The collapse narrative is being revised. While deforestation occurred, recent research suggests rats that arrived with settlers destroyed palm seeds, and European contact brought disease and slave raids that devastated the population more than internal environmental collapse.
